faq.q: What's the best budget motorcycle for UK touring?
faq.a: The Honda CB500X is probably the best all-rounder for budget UK touring at £6,500-£7,500 used. It's reliable, economical (65-70mpg), comfortable, and has excellent parts availability. The Suzuki V-Strom 650 and Kawasaki Versys 650 are also excellent choices at similar or lower prices.

faq.q: How much should I spend on a touring motorcycle?
faq.a: You can get a brilliant used touring bike for £4,000-£7,500. Japanese middleweights in this price range (V-Strom 650, CB500X, Versys 650) are proven, reliable, and perfect for UK conditions. Budget another £300-£500 for essential upgrades like luggage, heated grips, and a better screen.

faq.q: Are 500cc motorcycles big enough for touring?
faq.a: Absolutely. The Honda CB500X and similar 500cc bikes are perfect for UK touring. They handle motorways fine (if not thrillingly), return excellent fuel economy, are cheap to insure, and are light enough to manage easily. You don't need a big bike for British roads.

faq.q: What should I look for when buying a used touring bike?
faq.a: Check for complete service history, inspect for crash damage (bent levers, scraped cases, misaligned panels), examine tyre and chain condition, and look for useful extras already fitted. Bikes with crash bars, luggage, and heated grips already installed offer better value than stock ones.

faq.q: How much does it cost to run a budget touring motorcycle?
faq.a: Expect £280-£380 annually for insurance on a middleweight, £20-£25 fuel per 200 miles, £150-£250 per annual service, and £250-£350 per tyre set (lasting 8,000-10,000 miles). Japanese bikes are cheapest to maintain, with parts widely available and lower labour costs.

content:
Best Budget Touring Motorcycles UK: Affordable Bikes That'll Take You Anywhere

I've spent years touring Britain on everything from premium adventure bikes to scrappy little budget machines, and I'll tell you straight – you don't need to drop £10,000+ to explore every brilliant corner of this country. Some of my best tours have been on bikes that cost less than a decent used car.

The truth is, Britain's roads are perfect for budget touring bikes. We're not talking massive motorway slogs here – we're navigating tight Welsh valleys, Scottish single-tracks, and Pennine passes where a lighter, more manageable bike often beats the big-budget heavyweight. I've ridden the NC500 on a Versys 650, toured the Lake District on a CB500X, and crossed from coast to coast on a V-Strom 650. None of them broke the bank, and all of them delivered.

Let me walk you through the bikes I'd actually recommend spending your money on in 2026, plus what you need to know before you buy.

What Makes a Good Budget Touring Bike?

Before we dive into specific models, let's be clear about what matters for UK touring. I've learned this through plenty of wet miles and the odd breakdown.

The Non-Negotiables

First up, reliability. You need a bike that'll start on a damp morning in Fort William after sitting overnight. Japanese manufacturers dominate this space for good reason – Honda, Suzuki, Kawasaki, and Yamaha have decades of building bulletproof middleweights.

Weather protection matters more here than almost anywhere else. I've been caught in horizontal rain crossing the A66, and proper wind protection isn't a luxury – it's essential. Look for bikes with decent fairings or screens you can upgrade easily.

Comfort over distance is crucial. A sporty riding position feels great for an hour but murders your wrists and back after four hours of A-roads. I need upright ergonomics, a comfortable seat (or at least one I can replace), and pegs that don't cramp my knees.

Luggage capacity separates a tourer from a commuter. You need panniers or the ability to fit them. Soft luggage works brilliantly on a budget, but your bike needs mounting points or a decent subframe.

Running Costs Matter

It's not just the purchase price. I factor in insurance (which skyrockets above 650cc for many riders), fuel economy (critical when you're covering 300+ miles in a day), tyre costs, and service intervals. The best budget touring bike is one you can actually afford to run and maintain.

My Top Budget Touring Motorcycles for 2026

Honda CB500X (£6,500-£7,500 Used)

I'll be honest – this is probably my top pick for budget UK touring. The CB500X isn't exciting on paper, but it's bloody brilliant in practice. The 471cc parallel twin produces enough grunt for motorway work (just about) while returning 65-70mpg on tour.

I've ridden a 2022 model through the Brecon Beacons and up to the Scottish borders, and it handled everything brilliantly. The upright position is spot-on, the 19-inch front wheel copes with rough surfaces, and there's decent weather protection from the screen.

The seat's a bit firm for my liking beyond three hours, but that's a £150 fix with an aftermarket option. What sold me is how manageable it is – at 196kg wet, you can actually pick it up if (when) you drop it on a muddy verge. Try that with a 250kg adventure bike.

Parts are everywhere, servicing is cheap, and you can find crash bars, panniers, and screens all day long from SportsBikeShop. Insurance is reasonable because it's under 500cc.

Suzuki V-Strom 650 (£4,000-£6,500 Used)

The V-Strom 650 is the Swiss Army knife of budget touring. I know three riders who've taken these across Europe, and they're still running strong after 60,000+ miles. The 645cc V-twin has been around since 2004 with minimal changes because Suzuki got it right first time.

What I love about the DL650 is how effortless it makes touring. The engine pulls smoothly from 2,000rpm, perfect for lazy progress through the Yorkshire Dales or grinding up Scottish glens. Fuel economy sits around 55-60mpg, and the 20-litre tank means proper range between fill-ups.

The 2017+ models get better electronics and LED lights, but even the older versions are solid. I rode a 2014 model on the complete NC500 route and never wanted for anything except maybe a softer seat (there's a theme here).

Used V-Stroms are everywhere because people buy them, tour on them, then upgrade to something shinier. That means bargains if you're patient. Look for one with luggage already fitted – previous owners often spec them up nicely.

Kawasaki Versys 650 (£4,500-£7,000 Used)

The Versys shares its engine with the ER-6 and Ninja 650, so you're getting a proven parallel twin that's been refined over years. I borrowed a mate's 2020 Versys for a week-long Scottish tour, and I nearly bought one afterwards.

The handling is more road-focused than the V-Strom, which suits me fine because 90% of my touring is on tarmac anyway. It carves through the twisties brilliantly – I had a blast on the B840 along Loch Fyne. The adjustable screen works better than most, and the upright position is comfortable for all-day riding.

Fuel economy is excellent (60-65mpg), and the bike feels lighter and more flickable than its 216kg suggests. The main downside is ground clearance – if you're planning serious green-laning, look elsewhere. For road touring, though, it's spot-on.

The Versys also has a massive aftermarket support. Heated grips, crash protection, better seats, higher screens – you can spec one up exactly how you want it without spending ridiculous money.

Yamaha Tracer 700 / MT-07 (£5,000-£7,500 Used)

Here's where things get interesting. The MT-07 isn't marketed as a tourer, but with the right additions, it's brilliant. The Tracer 700 is the factory touring version with a screen, panniers, and more weather protection.

That 689cc parallel twin is a gem – punchy, characterful, and surprisingly efficient at around 60mpg. I've toured Wales extensively on an MT-07 fitted with soft luggage, and the only limitation was wind blast above 70mph. The Tracer solves that.

The chassis is brilliant for British B-roads. I've ridden from the Isle of Wight to the Highlands on a Tracer 700, and the balance of comfort and fun is perfect. It's genuinely entertaining on a twisty road while still eating miles when you need it to.

Watch for the 2020+ models with the updated dash and styling, though the earlier ones are mechanically identical and cheaper. The seat's decent (finally!), and the riding position works for riders from 5'7" to 6'2".

Royal Enfield Himalayan (£4,000-£5,500 Used)

Right, this one divides opinion, but hear me out. The Himalayan isn't fast, refined, or particularly powerful. What it is, though, is simple, capable, and perfectly suited to UK touring at a relaxed pace.

I spent a week pottering around the Peak District on a 2023 model, and I got it. The 411cc single makes just 24bhp, but it's enough for A-roads at 60mph and lovely through town. Fuel economy is spectacular – I saw 70+mpg – and the minimalist approach means less to go wrong.

The Himalayan excels on mixed surfaces. Those single-track roads in the Highlands? The muddy car parks at trail cafes? The occasional byway? It handles them all without complaint. The long suspension travel soaks up our crater-filled B-roads beautifully.

It's not for everyone. If you're planning long motorway runs or need to keep up with sports bike mates, look elsewhere. But for gentle, exploratory touring where the journey matters more than the destination, it's genuinely charming. Plus, it's the cheapest bike on this list to insure and maintain.

Bikes to Consider (With Caveats)

There are a few other machines worth mentioning, though they come with asterisks.

BMW F-Series (F750GS, F850GS)

These push the budget ceiling at £8,000-£10,000 used, but if you can stretch, they're superb. I've borrowed a mate's F750GS a few times, and the build quality, comfort, and capability are a step above the Japanese competition. The parallel twin is smooth, the electronics are genuinely useful, and the ride quality is excellent.

The downside? Service costs are higher, parts are more expensive, and you'll worry more about dropping it. For your first touring bike or if money's tight, I'd stick with Japanese. But if you can afford it and want something special, the F-Series delivers.

Triumph Tiger 660

The newer Tiger 660 (from 2022) is a brilliant package – modern, smooth, well-equipped, and properly capable. Used ones are starting to appear around £7,000-£8,000, and they're worth considering if you want something more contemporary than a ten-year-old Japanese bike.

I've only ridden one for a day (Triumph UK press launch in Wales), but I was impressed. The triple engine is lovely, the electronics are good, and it feels premium. Just be aware you're paying a bit extra for the badge and newer tech.

Honda NC750X

The NC750X should be perfect for touring – practical, efficient, reliable. And it is all those things. But the engine feels uninspiring, and I personally found it a bit soulless. That said, I know riders who absolutely love them for long-distance practicality. The built-in storage where the tank would be is genuinely clever.

If you prioritise function over feeling and want something different, try one. They're often cheap used because people don't "get" them, which means bargains for those who do.

The best touring bike isn't the one with the most features or the biggest engine – it's the one that makes you want to ride it. Buy something reliable and comfortable that fits your budget, then spend the money you saved on fuel, accommodation, and actually going places.

What to Look for When Buying Used

Most budget tourers are bought used, so here's what I check before handing over cash.

Service History

I want to see regular servicing, ideally at a dealer or reputable independent. Touring bikes rack up miles quickly, so maintenance matters. If the service book is incomplete or missing, walk away unless the price reflects it.

Obvious Damage

Crash damage happens, but I want to know about it. Check for misaligned panels, scraped engine cases, bent levers, and replaced parts. Minor cosmetic damage from a slow-speed drop is fine and gives you negotiating room. Major structural or frame damage is a hard no.

Tyres and Chain

These tell you how the bike's been maintained. Worn tyres or a rusty chain suggest neglect. Budget for replacements if needed – a new chain and sprockets costs £150-£250, and decent touring tyres are £250-£350 a set fitted.

Extras and Modifications

A bike already fitted with crash bars, luggage, heated grips, and a better screen is worth more than a stock one. Previous touring owners often spec bikes up nicely, then sell them at prices that don't reflect the added value. That's where you find bargains.

Essential Upgrades for Budget Touring

Once you've bought your bike, here's where I'd spend money first.

Luggage

Decent soft luggage costs £100-£200 and transforms a bike into a proper tourer. I use Kriega or Oxford – both are waterproof, durable, and expandable. Hard luggage is better long-term but costs £400-£800. Start soft, upgrade later if you tour regularly.

Screen

An aftermarket screen makes a huge difference to comfort. I've fitted higher screens to most bikes I've owned, and the reduction in wind buffeting transforms long days. Budget £80-£150.

Heated Grips

Non-negotiable for UK touring beyond June. Oxford heated grips cost £35 and fit any bike. They're genuinely transformative on cold mornings in Scotland or wet days in Wales. I've fitted them to every bike I've owned.

Tank Bag

For maps, phone, snacks, and wallet. Magnetic ones (if your tank is steel) are quickest on/off, but strap-mounted work for plastic or aluminium tanks. Budget £50-£100.

Running Costs and Practicalities

Let's talk real numbers because the purchase price is just the start.

Insurance

Bikes under 500cc are cheapest to insure. My CB500X costs £280 fully comp at 38 with full no-claims. A V-Strom 650 costs me £320. A Tracer 700 (technically a naked derivative) costs £380. Your age, location, and history obviously affect this, but middleweights are generally reasonable.

Fuel

At current fuel prices (around £1.45/litre in 2026), budget £20-£25 for 200 miles on a middleweight tourer. That's based on 60mpg average. It's not cheap, but it's manageable.

Servicing

Annual services cost £150-£250 at an independent, more at a dealer. Major services (valve checks, etc.) can hit £400-£600 but only happen every 12,000-24,000 miles depending on the bike. Japanese bikes are cheaper to service than European ones.

Tyres

Budget £250-£350 per set fitted. How long they last depends on riding style and mileage, but I typically get 8,000-10,000 miles from a set of touring tyres. Michelin Road 5s and Bridgestone T32s are my go-to choices.

Planning Your First Budget Tour

Once you've sorted your bike, use our route planning tool to map out your first proper tour. I'd recommend starting with a long weekend somewhere like the Lake District or Snowdonia – three days, 500-700 miles total, manageable distances each day.

Check out our packing checklist guide to make sure you've got everything you need without overloading your budget bike. Remember, lighter is better, especially on a smaller machine.

Weather prep is crucial. I've been soaked on tours in every month of the year, so pack proper waterproofs, even in summer. A good jacket and trousers cost £200-£400 but last years. Don't cheap out here – being cold and wet ruins tours.

Final Thoughts: Just Get Out There

I've toured Britain on bikes costing £3,000 and bikes costing £15,000, and honestly? The budget bikes delivered some of my favourite trips. There's less pressure, less worry about damage, and more focus on actually enjoying the ride.

My genuine recommendation? Buy a used CB500X, V-Strom 650, or Versys 650 with service history, add heated grips and soft luggage, and start exploring. You don't need more bike than that for UK touring. You need waterproofs, decent riding gear, and the willingness to just point yourself somewhere interesting.

The roads are waiting. The Lakes, the Highlands, the Welsh valleys, the Yorkshire Dales – they don't care what you're riding, as long as you show up. Budget bikes get you there just as reliably as premium ones, often more comfortably, and always with less stress about where you park overnight.

Get yourself a reliable middleweight, book a few days off work, plan a route, and go. That's what touring's about. See you out there.
